source.title: Parameters vs FLOPs: Scaling Laws for Optimal Sparsity for Mixture-of-Experts Language Models
source.authors: Samira Abnar; Harshay Shah; Dan Busbridge; A. Ali; Josh M. Susskind; Vimal Thilak

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures pretraining loss across model sizes, sparsity levels and compute budgets in MoE language models, testing compute-optimal allocation and a sparsity-aware scaling fit with methods different from the original dense-model studies.
record.gate_note: The study reports results on compute-optimal MoE configurations, sparsity-aware loss fits, and downstream performance relative to pretraining loss. Cited findings from other work are not recorded as results. The CoT experiment concerns inference-time compute, not the claim’s pretraining scaling relationship.
record.test_reason: The study trains sparse MoE language models from 3e19 to 1e21 FLOPs and applies Hoffmann-style IsoFLOP analysis and a Kaplan/Chinchilla-style parametric loss fit with a sparsity term. It also relates few-shot downstream error to pretraining loss. This puts the claim in a new architectural setting, with its own results on V1, V3, V6 and V7.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that, at fixed training FLOPs, raising MoE sparsity while enlarging total parameters lowers pretraining loss and cuts active parameters. Optimal sparsity rises with model size. Downstream performance tracks pretraining loss regardless of sparsity, except that denser models transfer better on reading comprehension. They also report that MoEs gain more from chain-of-thought inference compute (Qwen1.5 GSM8k), and they propose a sparsity-aware parametric scaling law.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains sparse MoE language models and analyzes loss with joint polynomial IsoFLOP surfaces and a sparsity-aware parametric form. The original sources analyze dense-model scaling and compute-optimal parameter/token allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary with sparsity, total model size, training compute budget and downstream task category. The study compares joint IsoFLOP surfaces with independent quadratic fits and reports qualitatively consistent trends.

fits_no_version.finding: At fixed total N and compute, loss is parabolic in sparsity. Optimal sparsity rises with N toward 1, and models below about 500M parameters are best dense. At fixed compute, the optimal loss falls monotonically with sparsity.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For MoEs, compute-optimal sparsity grows with model size, and sparser compute-optimal models reach lower pretraining loss.

record.problems: The study uses theoretical FLOPs and does not account for memory or communication overhead. The 98% sparsity held-out validation has R² 68%. Several trends are qualitative or presented in plots without uncertainty estimates, and the study does not fit compute-optimal parameter/token counts to powers of compute.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant reported results intentionally omitted. The CoT experiment in Appendix E measures inference-time compute effects and is not a result on the listed pretraining-scaling versions.

untested.parts: Dense-model laws over several orders of magnitude in compute. Compute spans only 3e19–1e21, and the law is fitted only to compute-optimal MoE runs.
Not tested. There is no prediction of runs orders of magnitude larger; held-out validation is in sparsity, not scale.
Exponents of N* and D* in C, compute-optimal token counts, and a Kaplan versus Hoffmann comparison.
Not tested. Depth and width at fixed parameter count are not compared; sparsity is treated separately.
Not tested. There are no other modalities, no repeated data, and no fine-tuning or transfer regimes.
Loss-to-downstream mapping is shown qualitatively in figures only. No predictive fit or prediction across scale is given.
Schedule, data and fitting-method effects on exponents. Published laws are not compared.

missing.what: Numeric compute-optimal total parameters N* per budget and sparsity from the independent quadratic fits. Dense, per the legend: about 330M (3e19), 509M (6e19), 658M (1e20), 1.3B (3e20), 2.9B (1e21). These imply an exponent of roughly 0.6, which no row records.
Held-out MSE of the IsoFLOP surfaces per compute budget (0.0000–0.0011), and 0.0001 for the Figure 1 fits.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V7 'challenges' label is dropped: R8 compares only trend directions, not fitted values. R4, R5 and R7 concern optimal sparsity, not the N/D split. The paper contradicts itself on how S* changes with compute (D.2: decreases; Discussion: increases). The CoT experiment uses Qwen1.5 models and is unrelated to any version. Neither is an original source.

versions.untested_parts: The study fits and validates a sparsity-aware parametric form on MoE pretraining data; it does not independently establish the original dense-model power laws over several orders of magnitude for parameters, tokens or compute.
Held-out validation excludes the 98% sparsity data, but the study does not test whether fits from small runs predict runs orders of magnitude larger.

The study reports qualitative changes in compute-optimal parameter counts and sparsity, but does not fit parameter-count or token-count exponents as powers of compute, nor report compute-optimal token counts as a function of compute.
The study does not compare depth, width or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
The study concerns text pretraining of MoE language models; it does not test other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning or transfer as training regimes.
The downstream relationship is tested on a selected few-shot benchmark suite, not broadly across downstream task types or model families.

The study compares its joint IsoFLOP-surface fit with independent quadratic IsoFLOP fits, but does not vary parameter-counting rules, data, training schedules, or other fitting choices, and does not test whether published laws disagree.

rows.subject: Pretrained MoE models (aggregate across fitted training data)
rows.operation_detail: Fit the proposed sparsity-aware parametric loss form L(N,D,S) using L-BFGS and Huber loss.
rows.measure: Pretraining categorical cross-entropy loss fit; reported fit-set MSE 0.00056, Huber loss 0.0036, and R² 99%; fitted α=0.5962, β=0.3954, λ=-0.1666, δ=0.1603, γ=0.1595.
rows.note: The fitted form includes power terms in parameters and tokens, plus sparsity and interaction terms; it is not a direct test of the original dense-model law.
rows.check: State should be observed: the power-law-plus-sparsity form fits the fitting set with R² 99% (MSE 0.00056). The tested range is limited: total N is roughly 50M–50B, tokens about 50B–400B, and compute spans about 1.5 orders of magnitude.

source_check.locator_found: Section 5, Equation 6 and Figure 6(a); Appendix F, paragraph preceding Table 2.

rows.subject: Pretrained MoE models (aggregate across held-out data)
rows.operation_detail: Validate the fitted sparsity-aware parametric loss form on data excluded from fitting.
rows.measure: Pretraining loss prediction; held-out MSE 0.0058, Huber loss 0.0011, and R² 68%.
rows.note: The paper reports this as out-of-sample validation; the held-out set is a sparsity condition, not runs orders of magnitude larger.
rows.check: Held-out R² is 68% on S=0.98, a different sparsity, not larger runs. This is extrapolation in sparsity, not scale, so it does not bear on V2.

source_check.locator_found: Figure 6(b) and caption; Appendix F, paragraph preceding Table 2.

rows.subject: Pretrained MoE models (aggregate across fitted configurations)
rows.operation_detail: Use fitted IsoFLOP surfaces to find compute-optimal total and active parameter counts across sparsity levels.
rows.measure: Compute-optimal total parameters N* and active parameters Na*
rows.value: N* increases and Na* decreases as sparsity increases.
rows.note: The text describes the trend; individual fitted values are shown graphically.
rows.check: The row reports how the compute-optimal size shifts with sparsity at one budget (1e20), not growth with compute. For V3 this is partial: the optimal size depends on sparsity, and no exponent is given. It also bears on V7: counting total versus active parameters gives opposite trends.

source_check.correct: V7: observed. V3: cannot_determine; remove the V3 link. At C=1e20 FLOPs, increasing sparsity increases optimal total parameters and decreases optimal active parameters. This comparison does not measure growth as a power of compute.
source_check.problem: The shared partial state conflates an observed V7 dependence with a fixed-budget comparison that cannot establish V3.

rows.subject: Pretrained MoE models (aggregate across fitted configurations)
rows.operation_detail: Find the loss-minimising sparsity for fixed total parameter count and compute budget.
rows.measure: Optimal sparsity S* as a function of total parameter count N
rows.value: S* increases with N and approaches 1.0 for larger models; models below a compute-dependent threshold can be harmed by increasing sparsity.
rows.note: The paper reports a qualitative trend and a threshold, not a power-law fit.
rows.check: Optimal sparsity versus total N is not a parameter/token split as a power of compute. Moved to fits_no_version.

rows.subject: Pretrained MoE models (aggregate across fitted configurations)
rows.operation_detail: Analyze the optimal sparsity as training compute changes for fixed model size.
rows.value: Increasing compute generally reduces S* at a fixed model size; for models up to about 500·10^6 parameters, S* is 0 for most compute budgets.
rows.note: The reported trend is qualitative and does not establish a power exponent.
rows.check: Same problem as R4: this is optimal sparsity, not the N/D split. The paper also contradicts itself. Appendix D.2 says S* generally falls with compute at fixed N, while the Discussion says S* rises with compute.

rows.subject: Pretrained MoE models (aggregate across fitted configurations)
rows.operation_detail: Compare compute-optimal total and active parameter counts across training compute budgets.
rows.measure: Compute-optimal total parameters N* and active parameters Na*
rows.value: Larger compute budgets shift the optimal total and active parameter counts upward at fixed sparsity.
rows.note: The study reports the direction of change but does not fit the counts to a power of compute.
rows.check: Optimal N and Na rise with compute at fixed sparsity, which is the V3 direction. No power or exponent is fitted, and token counts are not reported. Figure 12 legends give numeric N* values that no row records (see missing).

source_check.correct: V3: cannot_determine. Optimal total and active parameter counts increase with compute at fixed sparsity, but stable powers of compute for parameter and token counts are not established.
source_check.locator_found: Appendix D.4, first result bullet; Figure 12 and caption. The fitted-surface counterpart appears in Figure 9 and its caption.
source_check.problem: A qualitative increase does not establish either a stable power law or a measured weakening of that law.

rows.subject: Pretrained MoE models (aggregate across compute budgets)
rows.operation_detail: Compare optimal pretraining loss across sparsity levels at fixed training compute.
rows.value: Validation loss decreases as sparsity increases across all reported compute budgets.
rows.note: The paper says there is no significant difference in the slope of loss-versus-sparsity curves across the tested budgets.
rows.check: This row is about loss versus sparsity at fixed compute, an MoE architecture effect. It does not measure compute-optimal N/D allocation. Moved to fits_no_version.

rows.subject: Pretrained MoE models (aggregate across fitted configurations)
rows.operation_detail: Compare joint IsoFLOP-surface analysis with independent univariate quadratic IsoFLOP fits.

conditions.value: joint surface versus independent quadratic fits

rows.measure: Qualitative trends in optimal total and active parameters and optimal pretraining loss
rows.value: The independent fits reproduce the reported trends: increasing sparsity raises optimal total parameters, lowers optimal active parameters, and reduces optimal pretraining loss.
rows.note: This tests robustness to the two fitting approaches compared in the paper, not sensitivity to all setup or fitting choices.
rows.check: Joint-surface and independent quadratic fits agree only on the direction of trends. Fitted values or exponents are not compared between the two methods, so the row cannot show the presence or absence of fit-dependence as V7 defines it. The reader's 'challenges' label is unsupported.

relationships.condition: Compute-optimal MoE runs, 3e19–1e21 FLOPs, fitting set
relationships.reason: The Eq. 6 fit with power terms in N and D, plus sparsity terms, reaches R² 99% and MSE 0.00056 (R1).
relationships.display_finding: The loss fit combining parameter, data and sparsity terms achieved R² of 99% and mean squared error of 0.00056.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Compute-optimal MoE runs, 3e19–1e21 FLOPs, fitting set
source_check.reason: Equation 6 includes parameter and token power terms alongside sparsity terms; Appendix F reports fitting-set R²=99% and MSE=0.00056. Support is confined to this fitted, sparsity-aware form.

relationships.reason: The same parametric form predicts the held-out high-sparsity runs with only R² 68% (R2). An extra sparsity term is needed, and fit quality drops out of sample.
relationships.display_finding: At sparsity 0.98, held-out predictions reached only R² 68%, with an additional sparsity term needed.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.reason: The same fitted form has held-out R²=68% and MSE=0.0058 at S=0.98, qualifying its predictive adequacy across sparsities. This does not establish that an additional term is needed; sparsity terms are already included.

relationships.reason: Optimal total and active parameters rise with compute at every sparsity level, following the direction V3 states; no exponent is given (R6).
relationships.display_finding: Optimal total and active parameters rose with compute at every tested sparsity level.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.reason: R6 establishes increasing optimal parameter counts, but does not establish stable powers of compute for parameter and token counts. The untested power-law behavior cannot receive a supporting verdict from direction alone.

relationships.condition: Varying MoE sparsity at fixed compute
relationships.reason: The compute-optimal size depends on sparsity: sparser optimal models have more total and fewer active parameters, so more tokens (R3). The allocation is therefore not a single law across architectures.
relationships.display_finding: At fixed compute, greater sparsity shifted the optimum toward more total parameters, fewer active parameters, and more training tokens.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Varying MoE sparsity at fixed compute
source_check.reason: R3 compares sparsities at one compute budget. V3 does not require architecture-independent optimal sizes or coefficients, and this comparison does not show unstable allocation powers across compute budgets.

relationships.condition: Parameter counting in MoEs (total vs active)
relationships.reason: As sparsity rises, optimal total parameters increase while optimal active parameters decrease (R3). Which parameter count is used changes the compute-optimal conclusion.
relationships.display_finding: Increasing sparsity raised optimal total parameters while lowering optimal active parameters, changing the compute-optimal conclusion with the parameter-counting convention.

source_check.condition: Parameter counting in MoEs (total vs active)
source_check.reason: Figure 2 and Section 2.1 explicitly report opposite shifts in optimal total and active parameter counts as sparsity increases, supporting dependence on parameter counting and architecture.
